blocks.content: When you press the power button, your computer goes from a lifeless box to a running system in just a few seconds. Behind that moment is a careful chain of steps, each one waking up the machine a little more until the operating system is fully in charge.

This chain is called the boot process. It is worth understanding because it explains how a computer pulls itself up from nothing, loading the operating system into memory before you can do anything at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308714-305878837.png
1. When You Press Power

The moment you press power, electricity flows into the hardware, but the processor has no program to run yet. The operating system is still sitting on the disk, and the disk is not something the bare processor knows how to read on its own.

So the machine solves this step by step. It starts with a tiny program built into the hardware, uses that to load a slightly bigger program, and uses that to load the full operating system. Each stage bootstraps the next, which is where the word boot comes from.

["Pressing power sends electricity to the hardware","The processor has no program loaded yet","The operating system is still on the disk, not in memory","Each stage loads the next, bootstrapping up to the full system"]
items: Pressing power sends electricity to the hardware
The processor has no program loaded yet
The operating system is still on the disk, not in memory
Each stage loads the next, bootstrapping up to the full system

blocks.title: Pulling yourself up
blocks.content: The word boot comes from the phrase pulling yourself up by your bootstraps. The computer starts with almost nothing and loads bigger and bigger pieces until the whole operating system is running.
2. Firmware: BIOS and UEFI

The very first code to run is the firmware, a small program stored on a chip on the motherboard. Because it lives in the hardware itself, it is always there the instant the machine powers on, ready to take control.

On older machines this firmware is called the BIOS, and on modern machines it is called UEFI. UEFI is the newer replacement, with support for larger disks, faster startup, and better security, but both play the same role: the first program that runs and prepares the machine to boot.

["Firmware is code stored on a chip on the motherboard","It runs first, the instant the machine powers on","BIOS is the older name, UEFI is the modern replacement","Its job is to prepare the hardware and start the boot"]
items: Firmware is code stored on a chip on the motherboard
It runs first, the instant the machine powers on
BIOS is the older name, UEFI is the modern replacement
Its job is to prepare the hardware and start the boot

blocks.content: 3. POST: The Hardware Self Check

One of the first things the firmware does is run the POST, the Power On Self Test. This is a quick health check of the essential hardware, making sure the processor, memory, and key devices are present and working before going any further.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308714-74435677.png

If something critical is broken, the POST stops the boot and signals the problem, often with a pattern of beeps or an error on screen. If everything checks out, the firmware moves on to finding where the operating system lives.

["POST stands for Power On Self Test","It checks that the processor, memory, and devices work","A failure stops the boot and signals the fault","On success, the firmware moves on to find the boot device"]
items: POST stands for Power On Self Test
It checks that the processor, memory, and devices work
A failure stops the boot and signals the fault
On success, the firmware moves on to find the boot device

blocks.content: 4. Finding the Boot Device

Once the hardware passes its check, the firmware needs to decide where to boot from. A machine may have several storage devices, and the firmware follows a configured boot order to pick which one to try first.

It looks at the chosen device for a special startup area that holds the beginning of the boot software. This is why you can change the boot order in firmware settings to boot from a USB drive instead of the main disk, which is handy for installing a new operating system.

["The firmware follows a configured boot order","It checks each device for a bootable startup area","You can change this order to boot from USB or another disk","Once found, it loads the first piece of boot software"]
items: The firmware follows a configured boot order
It checks each device for a bootable startup area
You can change this order to boot from USB or another disk
Once found, it loads the first piece of boot software

blocks.title: Why boot order matters
blocks.content: Changing the boot order is how you install a fresh operating system. You tell the firmware to boot from the USB installer first, instead of the disk, so the installer runs before the old system.
5. The Bootloader
The small piece of code the firmware loads from the boot device is the bootloader. It is a specialised program whose whole job is to find the operating system kernel and load it into memory.

The bootloader is a middle step for a reason: the firmware is too simple to understand the operating system, and the kernel is too big to be started directly. The bootloader bridges that gap, and on many systems it also lets you choose between multiple operating systems at startup.

["The bootloader is loaded by the firmware from the boot device","Its job is to find and load the operating system kernel","It bridges the gap between simple firmware and the large kernel","It can offer a menu to choose between installed systems"]
items: The bootloader is loaded by the firmware from the boot device
Its job is to find and load the operating system kernel
It bridges the gap between simple firmware and the large kernel
It can offer a menu to choose between installed systems

blocks.title: The messenger
blocks.content: Think of the bootloader as a messenger. The firmware cannot read the operating system directly, so it hires this small, focused program to go and fetch the kernel for it.
6. Loading the Kernel
The bootloader now reads the kernel, the core of the operating system, from the disk and copies it into memory. This is the moment the real operating system enters the picture.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308714-564758039.png

Once the kernel is in memory, the bootloader hands over control to it and steps aside, its job complete. From this point on, the kernel is running the machine, and the firmware and bootloader are no longer in charge.
["The bootloader reads the kernel from disk into memory","It then hands control over to the kernel","The bootloader has finished its job and steps aside","The kernel is now in charge of the machine"]
items: The bootloader reads the kernel from disk into memory
It then hands control over to the kernel
The bootloader has finished its job and steps aside
The kernel is now in charge of the machine

blocks.content: 7. Kernel Initialisation
The kernel now sets itself up. This initialisation is a busy phase where the operating system prepares everything it needs to manage the machine and run programs.

It detects the hardware and loads the right device drivers, sets up how memory will be managed, and starts the scheduler that will share the processor among programs. By the end of this phase, the kernel is fully awake and ready to run software.
["The kernel detects hardware and loads device drivers","It sets up memory management","It starts the scheduler that shares the processor","By the end it is ready to run programs"]
items: The kernel detects hardware and loads device drivers
It sets up memory management
It starts the scheduler that shares the processor
By the end it is ready to run programs

blocks.title: Getting the house ready
blocks.content: Kernel initialisation is like a host preparing a house before guests arrive: turning on the lights, setting up the rooms, and getting everything ready so that when programs show up, they can be served right away.
8. The First Process
A kernel by itself does not do visible work, it manages programs. So near the end of startup, the kernel creates the very first process, the ancestor of every other program that will run.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308714-179172716.png

On many systems this first process is called init or systemd. Its job is to start everything else: the background services, the network, the logging, and eventually the login screen or desktop. Every process you ever run traces back to this single first one.
["The kernel creates the first process at the end of startup","It is often called init or systemd","It starts all the other services and programs","Every later process descends from this first one"]
items: The kernel creates the first process at the end of startup
It is often called init or systemd
It starts all the other services and programs
Every later process descends from this first one

blocks.content: 9. Reaching the Login

The first process starts the system services one after another: networking, logging, and all the background pieces that a running system needs. As these come up, the machine transforms from a bare kernel into a fully working environment.

Finally it starts the piece that greets you, the login screen or the graphical desktop. The boot process is now complete. Everything from the power button to this screen happened automatically, layer by layer, in just a few seconds.

["The first process starts services like networking and logging","The system becomes a full working environment","It then starts the login screen or desktop","The boot process is complete and the machine is ready"]
items: The first process starts services like networking and logging
The system becomes a full working environment
It then starts the login screen or desktop
The boot process is complete and the machine is ready

blocks.content: 10. Key Takeaways
